newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Primakov says NATO-Russia deal not certain in May.
newsitem.headline: Primakov says NATO-Russia deal not certain in May.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Sunday talks between Moscow and NATO this week would show whether the former Cold War foes can narrow their differences in time to sign a security deal on May 27.

But Primakov reiterated in a television interview that Moscow would sign nothing just for the sake of it and that he could not guarantee that his talks with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana in Moscow on Tuesday would solve all problems.
"There are still some loose ends, some issues which have to be resolved, and the negotiations will continue right until the end," Primakov told Russia Television in an interview recorded on May 8.
"But already on May 13 or 14, when General Secretary Solana is in Moscow, it will be clear whether we can get to sign the document on May 27 or not."
Asked if it was still possible an agreement would not be signed in Paris on the May 27 target date set by President Boris Yeltsin, Primakov replied: "I can't rule that out."
Yeltsin said last Thursday a document on Russia's relations with the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation was "98 percent" ready and he might join the next talks in Moscow to try to finalise the deal.
Russia opposes NATO's plans to expand eastwards to take in new members from the former Soviet bloc, saying such moves would threaten its security and open rifts in Europe.

But Yeltsin has signalled he wants a deal on terms for a new partnership with NATO, and as many concessions as possible, before the Western defence alliance issues the first new membership invitations at a summit in Madrid in July.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are thought to be top of the list to join, but Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new members.

Primakov failed to agree terms with Solana at talks in Luxembourg last week but said progress was being made. "The talks are hard. But I think we have moved quite a long way forward, although there are some questions which still have to be resolved, in particular on political and military matters," he told Russia Television.

In an interview in Monday's edition of the Izvestia newspaper, Primakov defended himself against criticism by some Russian media and politicians who say Moscow has nothing to show after months of negotiations with NATO.
"I must say that no one really appreciates what is being done (at talks) and what is being achieved," Primakov said.
"I want to reiterate that we are not pressed for time. We cannot sign a loose, ill-prepared document or one which does not suit us just because the French suggested the date of May 27."
He said he was victim of a campaign, conducted from inside and outside Russia, to weaken Moscow's negotiating stance.

The problems blocking agreement include a disagreement over how a treaty governing conventional weapons in Europe should be amended and whether a deal should contain a written NATO pledge not to move its military might into new member states.
Russia also wants a say in NATO decision-making but is unlikely to get this, even though the two sides have agreed to set up a joint council to discuss some matters.

A senior NATO official said last week the alliance was preparing a package of "sweeteners" to induce Moscow to drop its remaining objections, but made clear it could offer little more. "We are very close to our bottom line," the official said.
